project_scope.note: Built around the exact Erodium texanum video frame showing dissected foliage and the storksbill fruit. The species remains taxonomy/range-pending and is not a canonical target-zone anchor yet.
project_scope.reference_status: taxonomy/range review required before canonical install

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: For the local Erodium/Geranium pattern, find the persistent beak and five one-seeded mericarps of the mature schizocarp; confirm the flower center, then use leaf division to route genus. Do not use petal color alone or extend this exact pattern to all Geraniaceae.
family_diagnostics.fruit: A beaked schizocarp of five one-seeded mericarps is the standout family character in the familiar Geranium/Erodium pattern.
family_diagnostics.genus_tie_breaker: Geranium commonly has 10 fertile stamens, whereas Erodium commonly has 5 fertile stamens alternating with 5 staminodes.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Pink or purple five-petaled flowers are generic. The beaked five-part fruit is the structure worth memorizing.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant/leaf → five-part flower → beaked fruit → separated mericarp
visual_lesson.intro: Geraniaceae is a perfect family for learning from fruit: the storksbill/cranesbill mechanism is much more memorable than flower color.

steps.title: 1 · Notice the divided foliage
steps.photo_role: Erodium texanum dissected leaves / habit context
steps.look_for: Deeply divided or dissected foliage associated with the fruiting stem.
steps.why_it_matters: It provides useful whole-plant context, but foliage alone should not close the ID.

steps.title: 2 · Check the five-part flower
steps.look_for: Five sepals and five free petals.
steps.why_it_matters: This provides the floral framework shared across the familiar geranium relatives.

steps.title: 3 · Find the long beak
steps.look_for: An elongated beak rising above the developing or mature fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the fastest high-value visual cue supplied by the current Erodium video frame.

steps.title: 4 · Break the fruit into five
steps.look_for: Five one-seeded mericarps separating from a central axis, each with an awn that can coil or move as it dries.
steps.why_it_matters: The fruit architecture is the family-level confirmation and explains the cranesbill/storksbill look.

comparisons.title: Erodium vs Geranium
comparisons.rule: Use reproductive characters rather than leaf shape alone: Erodium typically has 5 fertile stamens plus 5 staminodes, whereas Geranium typically has 10 fertile stamens.

comparisons.title: Do not ID by petal color
comparisons.rule: Five free pinkish petals occur in many unrelated plants. The beaked schizocarp and five mericarps are much more informative.

visual_lesson.caveat: Erodium texanum is currently only a video-fed teaching reference pending strict taxonomy/range review. The family module can stay useful even if the species is not ultimately promoted.

genus_routing.cue: Usually pinnately divided leaves; five fertile stamens and five sterile staminodes; long-beaked fruit with twisting awns
Usually palmately divided leaves; typically ten fertile stamens; beaked five-mericarps fruit

confusable_families.separator: Oxalis has a five-locular capsule without the long stylar beak of local Geraniaceae
Linum has a capsule, sometimes with false septa, rather than a five-mericarps beaked schizocarp
